title: Four ways in which an 'agreement about the kinds of people we are helping our children and students become' can get in the way of learning.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton turns to the downside of a school's shared agreement about the kinds of people it is helping children become, the third factor affecting learning. He identifies four failure modes: an agreement too brief or vague to give clarity, one that has ossified as the community changes, one imposed on a community rather than built with it, and one that breeds cynicism because action does not match promises. Examples include taglines like developing 21st century learners, grammar schools resisting comprehensivisation, a royal Caribbean tour as an ossified curriculum, and an International Baccalaureate rollout done too quickly. He stresses that the process of shared development can matter more than the statement itself, citing a school that spent eighteen months consulting stakeholders. He ends with a checklist on clarity, currency, ownership and congruence.
points: Brevity should not beat clarity: a tagline is acceptable only when it follows a detailed, agreed account of the kind of children the school hopes to develop.
Ossification is a risk because school communities change, as his East End London school shows with its shifting pupil population.
An agreement imposed without wide discussion divides a school, so the process of building it with stakeholders matters as much as the text.
Congruence between stated purpose and daily behaviour keeps scepticism at bay, echoing Joe Murphy's two markers of good schools: focus on learning and consistency.
The post closes with a four-question checklist that mirrors the four failure modes.
quotes: What mattered most about ‘Great Learning, Great Teaching, Great Fun’ was that each of those three elements had substance behind them. Without that substance we were only creating uncertainty.

It does mean, though, that to really support learning, the tagline needs to come after a more detailed and agreed description of the kinds of children and students the school is hoping to develop so that the two are congruent.

Schools need to keep checking that their views about the kinds of children and students they are helping to develop remain vibrant and relevant to their community and their stakeholders. When they don’t, the world changes around them as does the learning needs of their children and students.

What went wrong was that the school’s thinking was a) too insular within the school, b) too far ahead of their stakeholders and c) imposed on but not discussed alongside the community. All three of these things caused learning to become unfocused and challenged.

What matters is that the stakeholders, in the school and outside it, have taken the time that is needed to work together to produce the agreement in the first place. When the statement is the community’s statement and not just the school’s its influence on learning can be supercharged.

In other words, their actions exemplify the vision and purpose they claim for their school. When you spend time in these schools, there is a consistency of behaviours wherever you go, a consistency that matches what the school says it believes in and how it wants its children and students to develop.

Making our views clear about the kinds of children and students we are helping to develop is an essential foundation for good learning but only if our behaviours and outcomes are visibly congruent with those views and consistent in their application.
